name: swift-collections (Deque)
baseline: Swift Array used as a queue, inserting at the front with insert(_:at: 0) (capacity reserved up front)
verdict_reason: In Apple's published raw data, prepending to a Deque stays flat per element while Array.insert(at: 0) grows linearly, reaching a gap of about 1,750x at 131,072 items. The cost is also in the data: random-access reads on a Deque are a few percent slower than on an Array at large sizes.
tier_reason: The benchmark library definition, run script (release build flags in Utils/run-benchmarks.sh) and raw results are in the repository, and the announcement post states the machine; only the Swift toolchain version is unstated.
claimed_speedup: Prepending Ints one at a time: at 131072 items the fastest run took 0.89 s for Array vs 0.000508 s for Deque, about 1,750x (derived from page data); at 1024 items 0.0000375 s vs 0.00000401 s, about 9.4x (derived from page data). Cost: random-offset reads over 1048576 items took 0.00546 s on Deque vs 0.00533 s on Array, about 2% slower (derived from page data). Times rounded to three significant figures from the raw results.
workload: Int elements; n prepends into an empty collection with capacity reserved (Array uses insert(i, at: 0)), and n subscript reads at random offsets; sizes 1 to 16M, 20 cycles; values above are the fastest recorded run per size, total seconds for the whole task.
toolchain: Release build (swift run -c release via Utils/run-benchmarks.sh); Swift version not stated (results committed April 2021, Swift 5.4 era)
platforms: All Swift platforms: iOS, macOS, tvOS, watchOS, visionOS, Linux, Windows
one_liner: Apple's ring-buffer double-ended queue; constant-time prepend and popFirst where Array.insert(at: 0) and removeFirst are linear.
how_it_is_fast: Deque stores elements in a circular buffer with a movable start index, so inserting or removing at the front only moves the start index instead of shifting every element. Array keeps elements contiguous from index 0, so every insert(at: 0) or removeFirst() moves the whole array. Deque keeps Array-style copy-on-write value semantics and integer indices.
use_it_when: FIFO queues or work lists where elements are added at one end and removed at the other (BFS, schedulers, sliding windows)
Any loop that calls insert(_:at: 0) or removeFirst() on an Array of more than a few hundred elements
Undo/redo or history buffers that trim from the front
skip_it_when: The collection is only appended to and read: Array is a little faster for random access and is contiguous
Code needs withUnsafeBufferPointer or contiguous storage for C or SIMD APIs; Deque storage can wrap around
Queues of a handful of elements, where the measured gap at 28 items is small
caveats: The announcement charts are images; the numbers here come from the raw results.json committed alongside them, using the fastest of the recorded runs per size, while the charts plot the 90th percentile.
Measured in 2021 on an Intel iMac Pro with an unstated Swift 5.x toolchain; Apple Silicon and newer compilers were not measured.
The Array baseline is insert(at: 0); Array.removeFirst(), the other common queue pattern, was not benchmarked here but has the same linear cost.
First-party benchmark by the library's authors.
tradeoffs: Storage is discontiguous, so there is no contiguous-buffer access and random reads cost a few percent more than Array

evidence.quote: were run on my 2017 iMac Pro.

This tends to make them work slightly slower than arrays for use cases that don’t call for inserting/removing elements at the front – so it’s probably not a good idea to blindly replace all your arrays with deques.
Mutations near the front are expected to be significantly faster in deques, but arrays may measure slightly faster for general random-access lookups.
